claims.text: Lattice and electronic thermal conductivity can be modeled as separate contributions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Machine-learning-trained force fields can capture static and dynamic local lattice distortions and use them to predict lattice thermal conductivity.
An electronic thermal-conductivity model based on refined plasma frequency and electron relaxation time can predict the electronic contribution independently.
The decoupled approach will reduce prediction error by approximately 50% relative to previous analytical methods.
The high-temperature comparison should use HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen to mirror published measurements.
Atomic-size and atomic-separation variations produce intrinsic local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Local lattice distortions alter vibrational modes and effective vibrational scattering.
Local lattice distortions do not directly perturb electronic conduction channels.
Changes in plasma frequency and relaxation time are relevant to conductivity in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Below 200 K, lattice heat transport dominates in HfNbTaTiZr.
The lattice contribution in HfNbTaTiZr will be nearly constant at low temperature.
The predicted low-temperature lattice contribution will closely match measurements below 200 K.
Electronic thermal conductivity will dominate HfNbTaTiZr heat transport between 300 and 1200 K.
Separating vibrational and electronic scattering mitigates cancellation errors caused by conflating the two mechanisms.
Existing DFT-and-analytical approaches have larger errors because they do not independently account for local-distortion effects on vibrational transport.
The approach is applicable to single-phase, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr and similar high-entropy alloys.
Polycrystallinity, secondary phases, and substantial extrinsic defects may compromise the approach's predictive accuracy.
Similar decoupled modeling in related high-entropy-alloy systems has produced improvements consistent with a roughly 50% error reduction.
